title: Of such is the kingdom (Luke 18:15–17)
hookLine: they bring even infants to be touched

cards: A crowd around a well-known teacher: serious men with serious questions about the law, the end of the age, money and the kingdom. And pushing in at the edges, parents carrying babies. Not toddlers who could ask questions.
Babies, swaddled, asleep, maybe crying. All the parents want is for him to lay his hand on them. To the disciples, it looks like a distraction.
You can almost hear them: not now, he's busy.

teach.b: Matthew and Mark tell this too, and their children are paidia, young children. Luke changes one word.
In the King James Bible: "And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them." Infants. In Greek, brephe, babies.

Luke used the same word for John the Baptist leaping in Elisabeth's womb, and for Jesus himself, the babe in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. These babies can't believe, or understand, or even ask to be brought.
Then: "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in old English, means allow. Let them come.
Then the line that turns it on the adults: "Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall in no wise enter therein." What does a baby do? It receives.
It's carried, fed, held. It doesn't earn anything. Luke puts this right after the tax collector who could only say God be merciful to me.
The same point twice: the kingdom isn't achieved, it's received. Christians apply this differently.
Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants, and some read this passage at baptisms.
Baptists and many others dedicate babies with a blessing and baptize those old enough to profess faith themselves.

teach.h: FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.
teach.b: Both hear the same thing: the youngest are not a distraction. They're the model.

how: Many churches baptize infants, including Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches, while Baptists and many others hold services of dedication and blessing for babies and baptize those who profess faith for themselves.

games.q: you're a disciple. Jesus is deep in teaching, and parents keep pushing forward with babies for him to touch. what do you do?
o: tell them off: not now, he's busy.
ask them to wait until the end.
games.why: the disciples rebuked them. "but Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not."

practice: Bring to mind a child you know, your own, a niece, a neighbor's baby, or the child you used to be, and hold them in your mind as if carrying them toward someone who loves them.
Wish them good things slowly: safety, kindness around them, room to grow. If you pray, pray for them by name; some families bless a child with a hand on the head or a sign of the cross at bedtime.

wordCard.voice: Brephe, Greek for infants, newborns: the babies the disciples tried to send away, and the ones Jesus says the kingdom belongs to.

orig.note: Greek: infants, babies. Luke's word here, the same one he uses for Jesus in the manger.

carryVoice: Your line: as a little child. Nothing to earn, only to receive. That's day five hundred sixty-five.
